idiom_name: one struct per node kind plus a kind tag and per-kind functions
implementation_notes: C has neither inheritance nor sum types, so the classic structure is written out by hand: a common header struct carrying the kind tag and token, plus one struct per node kind whose members are the named children (BinaryExpr { Expr *left; Token op; Expr *right; }). Payloads that differ in size hang off the node through a union or a per-kind struct, and every operation branches on the tag and downcasts to the concrete struct - the irregular child list the pattern prescribes. Keep it for hand-written C compilers, where it is the only option; if many generic passes are needed, build a normalized child array next to the named members for the walkers.
pitfalls: The downcast is only as safe as the tag: a wrong kind value, or reading a union member other than the one last written, is undefined behaviour.
Child pointers are owned manually: every node must be freed exactly once, and shared or cyclic subtrees need refcounts or an arena instead of plain malloc/free.
With no common child accessor, every walker repeats the tag switch and a newly added node kind is missed silently - there is no exhaustiveness check in C.
